concept.name: Measured move
concept.definition: A classical price-projection framework in which a trend leg, a corrective retracement, and a second trend leg are expected to be roughly equal in price (and, in the idealized version, in time): the second leg 'measures' the first. It is used both as a continuation pattern (a measured move up/down) and as a target-setting rule. It is a technical-analysis heuristic; empirical samples show the second leg typically falls short of the ideal.
concept.intuition: Markets often move in two similar thrusts separated by a pause; once you know the size of the first thrust and where the pause ended, you can estimate how far the second thrust should carry.
concept.mechanics: Identify three turning points: leg one from low A to high B, a corrective phase retracing part of that move to C, then a second leg from C toward D. Bulkowski's large-sample statistics: average first-leg rise 36% in 38 days, average retrace 48% in 27 days, average second-leg rise 31% in 33 days, with about 60% meeting the full price target; deeper retraces improve target achievement. The pattern also exists inverted (measured move down).
concept.formula: Price target = C + (B - A), where A = start (low) of leg 1, B = end (high) of leg 1 / start of the corrective phase, and C = low of the corrective phase; some practitioners scale (B - A) by the historical target-hit rate. For a measured move down: target = C - (A - B) with the corresponding peaks/troughs.
concept.failure_modes: The second leg fails to materialize when the corrective phase breaks down into a full reversal (price below C invalidates a measured move up); statistically the second leg undershoots the first by roughly a sixth on average. Overhead resistance or trend lines crossing the projected target frequently cap the move.
concept.misconceptions: That the second leg must equal the first in price and time — that equality is the idealized version; observed second legs are shorter on average, so the full measure is a reference, not an expectation.
concept.example: A stock rises from $20 (A) to $30 (B), retraces to $26 (C), then begins a second leg; the measured-move target is $26 + $10 = $36, and a drop back below $26 would invalidate the setup.
